title: Negotiation: ZOPA, BATNA & win-win
blurb: Plan and conduct a negotiation, and use ZOPA, BATNA and a win-win approach to reach a deal both sides can live with.
question: A leisure centre's project manager is about to negotiate with the preferred supplier of new gym equipment. The approved budget is £110k, the supplier has bid £125k, and a second supplier has also bid. How should the project manager plan the negotiation, and how do ZOPA, BATNA and a win-win approach help?

teach.h: Reaching a deal both sides can live with
teach.body: Negotiation is a discussion between two or more parties aiming to reach an agreement that each can accept. In procurement it settles price, scope, timescales, payment terms, risk and service levels with the preferred supplier. Plain English: each side wants something from the other, and negotiation finds terms you can both say yes to. Much of the result is decided before anyone sits down, in the planning.

steps.label: Plan & prepare
steps.sub: Objectives, priorities, walk-away point, BATNA, research

steps.label: Discuss & explore
steps.sub: Share interests, ask questions, test assumptions

steps.label: Agree & close
steps.sub: Confirm the terms and record them in writing

teach.caption: Recording the agreement matters: it becomes the basis of the contract and avoids later disputes.

children.sub: Ideal outcome, realistic target, walk-away point

children.sub: Must-haves versus things you can trade

children.sub: Yours, and your best guess at theirs

teach.caption: The ZOPA is where the two ranges overlap. Any agreed price must land inside it.

teach.h: ZOPA: the zone of possible agreement
teach.body: ZOPA is the overlap between each side's acceptable range: between the buyer's walk-away point (the most it will pay) and the supplier's walk-away point (the least it will accept). Any deal must land inside it. If the ranges do not overlap there is no ZOPA, so no deal is possible unless something changes, such as scope, timescales or payment terms, that widens one side's range. Estimating the ZOPA tells you how hard you can realistically push.

teach.h: BATNA: your best alternative to a negotiated agreement
teach.body: BATNA is what you will do if this negotiation fails: use the second-placed bidder, re-tender, do the work in-house or delay. It is your main source of power. A strong BATNA lets you walk away from a poor deal; a weak one means you need this deal more. Never accept terms worse than your BATNA, so it helps set your walk-away point. Improve it before you start (keep a second bidder interested) and estimate the supplier's BATNA too.

rows.label: Outcome
values: One side gains at the other's cost
Both gain what they value most

teach.caption: In iterative projects the buyer and supplier renegotiate priorities every time box, so protecting the relationship matters even more.

teach.h: Scenario: Riverside Leisure Centre's gym kit
teach.body: Riverside's budget limit is £110k (its walk-away point) and its BATNA is the second-placed bidder at £108k with a later delivery date. The preferred supplier opens at £125k. Exploring interests reveals that Riverside's real need is installation before its January opening, while the supplier wants cash flow and a showcase site. The deal: £103k, 40% paid on order, a case study for the supplier and installation guaranteed by mid-December. Both gain what matters most to them.

teach.text: Classic confusions. ZOPA is the OVERLAP of both sides' acceptable ranges, not your own range. BATNA is your ALTERNATIVE course of action if there is no deal (e.g. re-tender), not the deal itself; your walk-away point is set by comparing offers with your BATNA. Win-win does not mean splitting the difference or giving in: it means meeting both sides' underlying interests.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define BATNA and say how it helps: it gives you power and tells you when to walk away.
Define ZOPA and say how it helps: it shows whether a deal is possible and sets a realistic target.
Describe planning: objectives, priorities, walk-away point, research on the other side, concessions, roles.
Explain win-win: focus on interests not positions, so both gain and the relationship survives a long contract.
Tie each point to the scenario's supplier, budget and alternatives.
Stages: plan and prepare, discuss and explore, propose, bargain, agree and close (record it).
ZOPA: the zone of possible agreement, where both sides' acceptable ranges overlap.
BATNA: best alternative to a negotiated agreement; never accept less than it.
Win-win: principled negotiation on interests, not positions, protecting the relationship.
Most of the outcome is decided by the quality of the planning.

summary: You can now plan a negotiation and describe its stages from preparation to a recorded agreement. You can also explain ZOPA, BATNA and win-win and show how each helps a project manager get a good deal without damaging the supplier relationship.

options: Best Achievable Terms in a Negotiated Award
Buyer's Agreed Target for a New Agreement
Baseline Assessment of Terms Not Agreed
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
A.why: BATNA is the Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will do if no deal is reached.

whyNot.0: This sounds plausible but is not the term; BATNA is about your alternative if there is no deal.
whyNot.1: A target is part of your objectives; BATNA is your fallback option, not a target.
whyNot.2: This is invented wording; BATNA concerns your alternative course of action.

A.q: Which statement best describes the ZOPA in a negotiation?
options: The buyer's own full range of acceptable prices
The overlap between both sides' acceptable ranges
The option you will take if the negotiation fails
The first offer made by the stronger of the parties
A.why: ZOPA, the zone of possible agreement, is where the buyer's and the supplier's acceptable ranges overlap.

whyNot.0: One side's range alone is not the ZOPA; it is the overlap of both ranges.
whyNot.2: The option you take if talks fail is your BATNA.
whyNot.3: An opening offer is a tactic within the negotiation, not the zone of agreement.

A.q: In a typical negotiation, which stage comes FIRST?
options: Plan and prepare
Bargain
Propose
Agree and close
A.why: Negotiation starts with planning and preparation: objectives, priorities, walk-away point, BATNA and research on the other side.

whyNot.1: Bargaining (trading concessions) comes after proposals are on the table.
whyNot.2: Proposals come after preparing and exploring each side's interests.
whyNot.3: Agreeing and closing is the final stage.

B.q: Before negotiating with its preferred IT supplier, a retailer confirms that the second-placed bidder would still honour its tender. What has the retailer done?
options: Narrowed the zone of agreement
Set the supplier's walk-away point
Strengthened its own BATNA
Closed and recorded the agreement
B.why: Keeping the second bidder available gives the retailer a credible alternative if talks fail, which strengthens its BATNA.

whyNot.0: The ZOPA depends on both sides' ranges; securing an alternative strengthens BATNA rather than narrowing the ZOPA.
whyNot.1: Only the supplier can set its own walk-away point.
whyNot.3: Nothing has been agreed yet; the negotiation has not started.

B.q: A buyer will pay at most £40k. The supplier will accept no less than £48k. Neither will change any other term. What does this tell the negotiators?
options: No ZOPA exists, so no deal as things stand
The ZOPA is the range from £40k to £48k
The buyer's BATNA must therefore be £44k
They should simply split the gap at £44k
B.why: The buyer's maximum is below the supplier's minimum, so the ranges do not overlap: there is no ZOPA and no deal is possible unless something changes.

whyNot.1: £40k–£48k is the GAP between the ranges, not an overlap.
whyNot.2: BATNA is the buyer's alternative course of action, not a midpoint price.
whyNot.3: £44k is above the buyer's limit and below the supplier's, so neither would accept it.

B.q: Which of the following BEST reflects a win-win approach to negotiation?
options: Concede nothing until the other side gives in
Split every difference equally down the middle
Hide your priorities so you can't be exploited
Explore interests to find gains for both sides
B.why: Win-win (principled) negotiation explores both sides' underlying interests to find terms where both gain.

whyNot.0: Refusing to concede is a win-lose, positional tactic.
whyNot.1: Splitting differences is a compromise on positions; it may leave both sides' real interests unmet.
whyNot.2: Hiding everything blocks the problem-solving that win-win depends on.

C.q: A council is negotiating a 10-year facilities contract with a supplier it will work with daily. Its negotiator wants to squeeze every last penny using hard tactics. What is the BEST advice?
options: Go ahead, as the price is all that matters
Seek win-win terms to protect the relationship
Avoid negotiating and accept the bid as it is
Reveal the council's walk-away point at once
C.why: Over a long contract, goodwill and cooperation are worth a great deal. A win-win approach gets fair terms while protecting the relationship.

whyNot.0: Price matters, but a squeezed supplier may cut corners or claim hard on every change over ten years.
whyNot.2: Win-win still involves negotiating; it does not mean accepting the first bid.
whyNot.3: Revealing your limit straight away hands the supplier the advantage.

C.q: A project manager's BATNA is to hire the second-placed supplier for £90k. The preferred supplier now insists on £97k for an identical service. What should the project manager MOST likely do?
options: Accept £97k, as any deal beats no deal
Accept, as BATNA only matters to suppliers
Walk away and use the alternative supplier
Raise the BATNA to £97k so the deal fits
C.why: Never accept a deal worse than your BATNA. An identical service is available for £90k, so walking away is the better choice.

whyNot.0: A deal worse than your best alternative is not better than no deal.
whyNot.1: Both sides have a BATNA; the buyer's is what gives it the power to walk away.
whyNot.3: A BATNA is a real alternative, not a figure you can adjust to justify a worse deal.

C.q:
Which THREE of the following belong in planning and preparing for a negotiation?
1) Setting objectives and a walk-away point
2) Researching the other side's interests
3) Recording the agreed terms in writing
4) Identifying your BATNA
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
C.why: Objectives and a walk-away point, research on the other side and identifying your BATNA are all preparation. Recording the terms happens when you agree and close.

whyNot.0: Item 3 belongs to the agree-and-close stage, not planning.
whyNot.1: Item 3 belongs to agree and close, and this option leaves out research on the other side.
whyNot.2: Item 3 belongs to agree and close, and this option leaves out objectives and the walk-away point.

reteach.title: Buying a used car
reteach.question: You are buying a second-hand car from a private seller. Where are the ZOPA, your BATNA and the win-win in this everyday deal?

blocks.body: You would like to pay £6.5k but will go up to £8k (your walk-away point). The seller hopes for £8.5k but would take £7k. Between £7k and £8k is the ZOPA. A similar car you could buy down the road for £7.8k is your BATNA: it is why you won't pay £8.2k. Talking reveals the seller needs a quick sale before moving abroad, and you want the new tyres included. You agree £7.4k with the tyres, collected tomorrow. Both of you win.

blocks.h: The car deal on one line

blocks.text: The other car down the road is your BATNA, not your ZOPA. The ZOPA only exists because your range and the seller's range overlap.

explain.body: Plan and prepare, then discuss and explore interests, propose, bargain (trade concessions) and finally agree and close, recording the terms in writing.

test.q: During a negotiation, the buyer says: 'If you can deliver two weeks earlier, we can pay 30% on order.' Which stage is this?
options: Bargaining
Planning
Closing
Exploring
test.why: Trading one concession for another ('if you…, then we…') is bargaining.

whyNot.1: Planning happens before the parties meet.
whyNot.2: Closing confirms and records terms already agreed.
whyNot.3: Exploring is about understanding interests, before offers are traded.

explain.body: The zone of possible agreement is the overlap between what the buyer will accept and what the supplier will accept. Any deal lands inside it. No overlap means no ZOPA.

test.q: Complete the statement: the ZOPA is the range in which ___.
options: only the buyer is willing to settle
the supplier makes its opening offer
both parties could accept a deal
the negotiation is certain to fail
test.why: The ZOPA is the range where both parties' acceptable ranges overlap, so either could accept a deal there.

whyNot.0: The ZOPA needs both sides, not just the buyer.
whyNot.1: An opening offer is usually outside the other side's range, not the ZOPA.
whyNot.3: A ZOPA means a deal IS possible.

explain.body: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if talks fail. A strong BATNA gives you power to walk away; never accept a deal worse than it.

test.q: Why does a strong BATNA improve a negotiator's position?
options: It forces the other side to accept any offer
It lets them walk away from a poor deal
It guarantees that the ZOPA will be wide
It removes the need to plan the negotiation
test.why: With a good alternative available, the negotiator does not need this deal and can walk away from poor terms.

whyNot.0: A BATNA gives leverage; it cannot force the other side to accept anything.
whyNot.2: The width of the ZOPA depends on both sides' ranges, not on your BATNA alone.
whyNot.3: Identifying your BATNA is itself part of the planning.

explain.body: Principled (integrative) negotiation focuses on interests, not positions, so both sides gain something they value and the relationship is protected. It matters most when you will work together for a long time.

test.q: A win-win negotiation focuses mainly on which of the following?
options: Interests, not positions
Positions, not interests
Price, not relationships
Winning, not agreeing
test.why: Win-win negotiation looks behind stated positions to each side's underlying interests.

whyNot.1: Focusing on positions is the win-lose, haggling style.
whyNot.2: Win-win protects relationships rather than sacrificing them for price.
whyNot.3: Win-win is about reaching an agreement both sides value.
